analysis.one_liner: Permanently cuts the estate tax for the largest estates and removes taxes on small-business stock gains and government contractor payments.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on December 2, 2009, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make the estate tax permanently cheaper for large estates: a $5 million tax-free exemption, a top rate of 35%, an extra deduction of up to $5 million for family-owned businesses, and a $2 million deduction for the family home. It would also make all gains from qualified small business stock held more than five years tax-free and exempt that gain from the alternative minimum tax, and it would repeal the rule requiring governments to withhold 3% of payments owed to their contractors. None of the tax cuts were paired with any offsetting revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: The heirs of large estates would pay the least tax: a $5 million exemption per estate, a 35% top rate, and deductions for a family business and the family home mean estates worth up to roughly $12 million could escape estate tax entirely. Owners of small business stock would pay no tax on gains after five years, and government contractors would get the full amount of their invoices without a 3% set-aside.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Heirs of large estates and investors

how_it_helps.text: It would permanently exclude the first $5 million of an estate from tax and cut the top estate tax rate to 35%, permanently extending provisions of the 2001 tax law that were scheduled to expire.
It would let families deduct up to an additional $5 million for a family-owned business and $2 million for a decedent's principal residence from the taxable estate.
It would make 100% of the gain on qualified small business stock held more than five years tax-free and exclude that gain from the alternative minimum tax.
It would repeal the requirement that federal, state, and local governments withhold 3% of payments owed to their vendors.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would collect less revenue, leaving other taxpayers to make up the difference or adding to deficits; the burden of funding government services would tilt toward households that pay income and payroll taxes rather than estate taxes. Repealing the 3% withholding would also make it easier for some government vendors to avoid paying taxes they owe.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the estate tax rate to 35% and raising the exclusion to $5 million, plus a $2 million residence deduction, would reduce federal revenue and shift the tax burden toward households that never build multi-million-dollar estates.

Repealing the 3% withholding requirement on government payments would make it easier for contractors to underpay taxes owed, which the Government Accountability Office had identified as a tax-compliance problem.

A full income-tax exclusion for gains on small business stock held over five years, plus an AMT carve-out, primarily benefits investors who already hold such equity — a small, wealthy population — rather than the businesses' workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow to the very largest estates and to investors and contractors who would otherwise pay tax they owed; its costs land on federal revenues that fund services everyone relies on. It did not pair tax relief with any offsetting revenue, and the estate-tax cuts for households passing on $5-12 million are far larger in dollar terms than the small-business and principal-residence provisions that touch more people. As designed, the cost to the public outweighs the diffuse benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and no committee ever acted on it, so it died at the end of the 111th Congress without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 2, 2009, with no cosponsors, and referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee.
The committee took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report — and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Estate tax as it stood (temporarily repealed for 2010, then a 35% rate with a $5 million exclusion under the later 2010 compromise) plus the 3% vendor withholding survived being repealed only later; for this bill, the concentrated interests it targeted gained nothing, and no tax revenue was lost to it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply died

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup, hearing, or vote on the bill after referring it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors, and was never considered, so no partisan alignment was ever tested.

industries.industry: Very wealthy households and large estates
industries.note: The bill would permanently shield the first $5 million of each estate and cut the top estate tax rate to 35%, saving heirs of large estates substantial tax. Because it is permanent, it would lock in those savings year after year.

Owners of family businesses could deduct up to $5 million of business value from the taxable estate, easing succession. The benefit accrues mainly to the owners and their heirs rather than employees or customers.

Sellers of qualified small business stock held over five years would pay no income tax on the gain and would not face it under the alternative minimum tax. The benefit goes to existing equity holders, not to the businesses' workers.
Repealing the 3% withholding on government payments would free contractor cash flow, but would remove a mechanism designed to ensure those vendors actually pay the taxes they owe.
